title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove the minimum number of parentheses to make s valid and return all distinct valid strings.
Idea: level begins with {s}; validate every string and return the whole first valid level, otherwise generate strings by deleting one parenthesis while skipping repeated adjacent choices.
Technique and why it applies: Breadth-first search explores deletions by count, so the first level with valid strings uses the fewest removals.
Invariant: Every string in level has the same number of deletions from the original s.
Edge cases: Already-valid input returns unchanged; "()())()" has multiple shortest answers; letters are never deleted. The valid helper rejects a negative prefix balance and requires final balance zero.
Complexity: Time O(n*2^n), space O(2^n) strings.
complexity_reason: Each level may contain exponentially many strings, and valid scans each string while next_level stores generated candidates.

title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
notes:
Task and constraints: Return every distinct result after the minimum number of parenthesis deletions needed for validity.
Idea: Keep a HashSet level, collect all strings passing valid, and if none pass create next by removing one parenthesis at each nonduplicate adjacent position.
Technique and why it applies: BFS layers count deletions, ensuring the first valid layer is minimal; sets deduplicate identical strings.
Invariant: All strings in a level have undergone the same number of removals.
Edge cases: Valid input returns itself; repeated parentheses skip equivalent deletions; non-parenthesis characters are preserved. valid rejects negative balance and requires zero at end.
Complexity: Time O(n*2^n), space O(2^n) strings.
complexity_reason: The level and next sets can contain exponentially many strings, each valid check scans its characters.

title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
notes:
Task and constraints: Support repeated inclusive range-sum queries over an immutable integer array.
Idea: Build prefix with a leading zero and cumulative sums; sumRange subtracts prefix[left] from prefix[right+1].
Technique and why it applies: Prefix sums turn any interval total into the difference of two precomputed prefix totals.
Invariant: prefix[i] equals the sum of nums[0:i].
Edge cases: A single-index query returns that element; [0,n-1] returns the full sum; empty input can construct prefix=[0] but no valid index query exists.
Complexity: Construction O(n), query O(1), space O(n).
complexity_reason: Construction appends one cumulative total per input value, and each query performs one subtraction.

title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
notes:
Task and constraints: Preprocess nums for repeated inclusive sumRange(left,right) queries.
Idea: Allocate prefix of length n+1, set prefix[i+1]=prefix[i]+nums[i], and answer each query with prefix[right+1]-prefix[left].
Technique and why it applies: A prefix-difference query cancels all values before left and retains exactly the requested interval.
Invariant: prefix[j] is the sum of the first j input elements.
Edge cases: left==right returns one value; the full-range query uses prefix[n]; int prefix sums may overflow if the problem's total exceeds int range.
Complexity: Construction O(n), query O(1), space O(n).
complexity_reason: The constructor processes each value once and each query reads two prefix entries.

title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
notes:
Task and constraints: Answer inclusive rectangular matrix-sum queries after preprocessing.
Idea: Build a padded prefix table using top+left-current-overlap for every cell; sumRegion combines four prefix corners with inclusion-exclusion.
Technique and why it applies: A 2D prefix table stores every top-left rectangle sum, allowing four accesses to isolate any subrectangle.
Invariant: prefix[r+1][c+1] equals the sum of matrix cells from (0,0) through (r,c).
Edge cases: A one-cell region returns that cell; the whole matrix uses the padded corners; an empty matrix builds a 1x1 table but no valid region query exists.
Complexity: Construction O(mn), query O(1), space O(mn).
complexity_reason: The nested constructor loops fill mn prefix cells and each query performs four table lookups.

title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
notes:
Task and constraints: Precompute a matrix for constant-time inclusive rectangular sum queries.
Idea: Allocate padded pref, fill each pref[r+1][c+1] from matrix plus top and left minus overlap, then query using four-corner inclusion-exclusion.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix rectangles let the query subtract unwanted top and left areas and add back their overlap.
Invariant: pref[r+1][c+1] contains the sum of the rectangle from origin to matrix[r][c].
Edge cases: A one-cell query returns its value; the whole matrix uses all four boundary terms; int prefix sums may overflow if totals exceed Java int bounds.
Complexity: Construction O(mn), query O(1), space O(mn).
complexity_reason: Two nested loops fill the table and each query accesses four pref entries.

title: Additive Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether a digit string splits into at least three consecutive numbers where each later number is the sum of its previous two, bounded by 2^31-1.
Idea: Try first split i and second split j, reject leading-zero multi-digit parts and oversized seeds, then extend x,y by matching str(x+y) at pos.
Technique and why it applies: Enumerating the first two terms determines every later term, so matching the forced sum validates a candidate split.
Invariant: At each extension, num[:pos] is partitioned into a valid additive prefix ending with x,y.
Edge cases: Leading zero is allowed only as a single digit; a sum that does not match stops that split; fewer than three terms fail. Python ints do not overflow, so limit enforces the statement bound.
Complexity: Time O(n^3) worst case, space O(n).
code:
class Solution:
    def isAdditiveNumber(self, num: str) -> bool:
        n=len(num); limit=2**31-1
        for i in range(1,n):
            if num[0]=='0' and i>1: break
            a=int(num[:i])
            for j in range(i+1,n):
                if num[i]=='0' and j>i+1: break
                b=int(num[i:j])
                if a>limit or b>limit: break
                pos=j; x,y=a,b; count=2
                while pos<n:
                    z=x+y; text=str(z)
                    if z>limit or not num.startswith(text,pos): break
                    pos+=len(text); x,y=y,z; count+=1
                if pos==n and count>=3: return True
        return False
complexity_reason: The two split loops enumerate O(n^2) starts and each extension may scan/copy O(n) digits.

title: Additive Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether num is an additive sequence of at least three numbers, each at most Integer.MAX_VALUE.
Idea: Enumerate i and j up to ten digits, enforce leading-zero rules, parse seeds as long, and extend by matching each x+y string at pos.
Technique and why it applies: Once the first two numbers are chosen, every subsequent number is forced, reducing validation to sequential prefix matching.
Invariant: pos marks the end of a prefix satisfying the additive recurrence, with x and y the latest two values.
Edge cases: A multi-digit seed starting with zero is rejected; values or sums above Integer.MAX_VALUE stop that split; Long parsing is safe because seed lengths are capped at ten digits.
Complexity: Time O(n^3) worst case, space O(n).
complexity_reason: The split loops explore O(n^2) choices and substring/string comparisons can scan O(n) characters.

title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
notes:
Task and constraints: Support point updates and inclusive range sums on a mutable integer array.
Idea: Copy nums, initialize bit via _add; update computes delta from stored nums and adds it at index+1; sumRange subtracts _sum(left) from _sum(right+1).
Technique and why it applies: A Fenwick tree updates and queries prefix sums by jumping through indices using the low bit.
Invariant: bit entries store partial sums for their Fenwick index ranges, and nums tracks current values for update deltas.
Edge cases: Updating to the same value uses delta zero; a single-index query returns that value; invalid indices are not checked.
Complexity: Build O(n log n), update/query O(log n), space O(n).
time_complexity: O(n log n) construction; O(log n) update/query
complexity_reason: Each _add and _sum follows O(log n) low-bit jumps, and nums plus bit store n-scale arrays.

title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
notes:
Task and constraints: Maintain point values with update and inclusive range-sum queries.
Idea: Clone values into nums, initialize bit through add(i+1,value), apply update deltas at index+1, and calculate ranges from prefix(right+1)-prefix(left).
Technique and why it applies: Fenwick low-bit jumps update/query logarithmically many partial sums rather than scanning the array.
Invariant: nums contains current point values, while bit maintains the partial ranges required for prefix sums.
Edge cases: Updating an element to itself adds zero; left==right returns one value; int tree totals can overflow if problem bounds exceed int range.
Complexity: Build O(n log n), update/query O(log n), space O(n).
time_complexity: O(n log n) construction; O(log n) update/query
complexity_reason: Initialization calls add for each element and each update/prefix query follows logarithmic low-bit jumps.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize stock profit when selling forces a one-day cooldown before another purchase.
Idea: Save old_hold, old_sold, old_rest each day; hold either persists or buys from old_rest, sold comes from old_hold plus price, and rest keeps the better of old_rest and old_sold.
Technique and why it applies: Three-state DP separates holding, just sold, and cooldown-eligible rest so a sale cannot fund an immediate next-day buy.
Invariant: Each state stores the best profit for its named condition after processed prices.
Edge cases: Empty prices returns 0; a single day cannot profit; after a sale, buying on the immediately following day is blocked because hold uses old_rest.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop processes each price once and retains three state values plus their snapshots.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize profit over prices with a mandatory cooldown day after each sale.
Idea: Snapshot hold, sold, and rest as h,s,r; update hold from h or r-p, sold from h+p, and rest from r or s.
Technique and why it applies: Separate states encode whether a stock is held, was just sold, or is available for buying after cooldown.
Invariant: h, s, and r represent the best profits for their respective states before the current day's transitions.
Edge cases: Empty prices returns 0; one price returns 0; using snapshots prevents updated sold from incorrectly enabling a same-day state transition. The negative sentinel avoids buying-state initialization at zero.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop reads each price once and updates a fixed number of int states.

title: Minimum Height Trees
notes:
Task and constraints: Find all roots yielding minimum tree height in an undirected tree.
Idea: Return all vertices for n<=2; otherwise build adjacency sets, queue degree-one leaves, and repeatedly remove a whole leaf layer until at most two vertices remain.
Technique and why it applies: Repeated leaf trimming converges to the tree's center, which minimizes maximum distance to any vertex.
Invariant: leaves contains the current outer layer, and remaining counts vertices not yet removed.
Edge cases: n=1 or 2 returns all vertices; a path leaves its middle node or two middle nodes; input is assumed to be a tree, so disconnected graphs are not handled.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: Each vertex is removed once and each edge is processed a constant number of times.

title: Minimum Height Trees
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the center vertex or vertices of a tree that produce minimum height.
Idea: Build adjacency sets, queue all degree-one nodes, then remove layers while remain>2, removing each leaf from its neighbor and queueing newly exposed leaves.
Technique and why it applies: Tree centers remain after repeatedly peeling the outermost layer, minimizing maximum distance to a node.
Invariant: q holds leaves for the next layer and remain counts vertices not yet peeled.
Edge cases: n<=2 returns every vertex; a path has one or two center vertices; the code assumes a connected acyclic input. Clearing each removed leaf's set prevents stale adjacency.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: The queue removes each vertex once and adjacency sets store each tree edge at both endpoints.

title: Burst Balloons
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize coins from bursting balloons, where each burst scores the product of its current neighbors.
Idea: Pad nums with boundary ones, fill dp by increasing interval length, and try each k as the last balloon in [left,right], combining its score with optimal left/right intervals.
Technique and why it applies: Interval DP works by choosing the last burst, making the neighboring values fixed at the interval boundaries.
Invariant: dp[left][right] is the maximum coins obtainable by bursting exactly that interval while its outside boundaries remain.
Edge cases: Empty nums returns dp[1][0] which is zero; a single balloon scores its value; padding with ones handles boundary balloons.
Complexity: Time O(n^3), space O(n^2).
complexity_reason: The length, left, and last-k loops examine cubic interval choices and dp stores a quadratic table.

title: Burst Balloons
notes:
Task and constraints: Choose a burst order maximizing coins, with boundary values treated as one.
Idea: Copy nums into padded a, initialize dp, and for increasing interval length try every k as the last balloon, adding a[l-1]*a[k]*a[r+1] and both subinterval scores.
Technique and why it applies: Choosing the final balloon makes its neighbors the interval boundaries and separates the remaining work into independent intervals.
Invariant: dp[l][r] stores the best score for bursting balloons l through r last within those boundaries.
Edge cases: Empty nums returns dp[1][0], which is zero with the allocated table; a singleton uses both boundary ones; int products can overflow if constraints allow large products.
Complexity: Time O(n^3), space O(n^2).
complexity_reason: Three nested loops consider each interval and possible final balloon; dp stores O(n^2) states.

title: Super Ugly Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the nth positive number whose prime factors come only from the given primes.
Idea: Initialize dp[0]=1, keep one index and candidate product per prime, choose the smallest candidate for each next dp entry, and advance every prime pointer tied at that value.
Technique and why it applies: Multi-pointer DP merges sorted sequences of prime multiples while advancing ties to avoid duplicate numbers.
Invariant: vals[j] is primes[j] times the next dp value not yet consumed by that prime.
Edge cases: n=1 returns 1; multiple primes may generate the same candidate and all tied indices advance; empty primes with n>1 would fail at min(vals), outside expected input.
Complexity: Time O(n*p), space O(n+p).
complexity_reason: Each of n outputs scans p candidate values and dp, idx, and vals store O(n+p) items.

title: Super Ugly Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the nth super ugly number using only the supplied prime factors.
Idea: dp starts at 1; each step finds the minimum val candidate, stores it, and advances every index whose prime product equals that minimum.
Technique and why it applies: Multi-pointer dynamic programming merges the multiples generated by each prime in sorted order.
Invariant: val[j] is the next not-yet-emitted multiple of primes[j], and idx[j] points into dp for that candidate.
Edge cases: n=1 returns 1; ties advance every matching prime to prevent duplicate sequence entries; long val prevents intermediate multiplication overflow, but final dp values must fit int.
Complexity: Time O(n*p), space O(n+p).
complexity_reason: Each output scans p candidates and each prime keeps one index and one long candidate.

title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
notes:
Task and constraints: For each nums[i], count strictly smaller values to its right.
Idea: Sort (index,value) pairs recursively; while merging, count how many right-half values have passed and add that count to ans for each left item before writing merged pairs back.
Technique and why it applies: Merge-sort counting uses the sorted right half to count smaller elements efficiently across halves.
Invariant: During merge, j counts right-side values already emitted that are smaller than the current left value.
Edge cases: Empty input returns []; equal values are not counted as smaller because left wins on <=; a descending array accumulates many smaller-right counts.
Complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: Merge sort processes each element at each recursion level and stores pair lists plus merge buffers.

title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
notes:
Task and constraints: Count, for each index, later values strictly smaller than nums[i].
Idea: Sort indices by nums through sort(l,r); during merge, increment passed when a right value is smaller, add passed to ans for each left index, and copy tmp back into idx.
Technique and why it applies: Merge-sort ordering makes all right values already passed smaller than the current left value.
Invariant: passed is the count of right-half elements emitted before the current left item, and each ans is accumulated across merge levels.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list; equal values are not counted because the right branch requires strict <; negative values are ordered normally.
Complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: Each merge level processes all indices once, and idx, tmp, and ans each contain n entries.
